exam_name: ISTQB Certified Tester Testing with Generative AI

questions.question: What is "zero-shot prompting"?

options.D: Asking the model to perform a task with no worked examples in the prompt
options.A: Asking the model to answer with zero tokens, which does not hold here
options.B: Running the model with zero temperature, which is a frequent misreading
options.C: Testing the model without any input at all, though it misses the actual cause

questions.explanation: This reflects the underlying mechanism: asking the model to perform a task with no worked examples in the prompt.

questions.question: What is a "decoding strategy" in text generation?

options.C: The method used to choose the next token from the model's predicted probabilities, such as greedy or sampling
options.A: The process of translating output into another language, which conflates the symptom with the underlying cause of the problem
options.B: A way to compress the model file, which overlooks the actual mechanism driving the behaviour being tested
options.D: The encryption method for API responses, which confuses two separate concepts

questions.explanation: This reflects the underlying mechanism: the method used to choose the next token from the model's predicted probabilities, such as greedy or sampling.

questions.question: What best describes an "instruction-tuned" model?

options.B: A base model further trained to follow natural-language instructions and prompts more reliably
options.A: A model that can only be used by developers with instructions, which confuses two separate concepts
options.C: A model tuned solely to run faster, as some teams mistakenly believe
options.D: A model restricted to a single instruction per session, though it misses the actual cause

questions.explanation: This reflects the underlying mechanism: a base model further trained to follow natural-language instructions and prompts more reliably.

questions.question: What is a "multimodal" GenAI model?

options.A: A model that can accept and/or generate more than one type of content, such as text and images
options.B: A model deployed across multiple servers, which confuses two separate concepts
options.C: A model with multiple API keys, a reasonable-sounding guess that does not survive scrutiny in practice
options.D: A model that only works in multiple languages, though it misses the actual cause

questions.explanation: This reflects the underlying mechanism: a model that can accept and/or generate more than one type of content, such as text and images.

questions.question: What does "grounding" mean for a GenAI response?

options.D: Anchoring the response in verifiable external information, such as retrieved documents
options.A: Reducing the temperature to zero, which overlooks the actual mechanism driving the behaviour being tested
options.B: Disconnecting the model from the internet, though it misses the actual cause
options.C: Formatting the answer as plain text, which confuses two separate concepts

questions.explanation: This reflects the underlying mechanism: anchoring the response in verifiable external information, such as retrieved documents, rather than relying only on internal parameters.

questions.question: What happens during model "inference"?

options.D: The trained model processes an input and produces an output, without updating its weights
options.A: The model's weights are updated from new training data, based on a common misconception
options.B: The model is compiled into machine code, which confuses two separate concepts
options.C: The model's training data is deleted, which conflates the symptom with the underlying cause of the problem

questions.explanation: This reflects the underlying mechanism: the trained model processes an input and produces an output, without updating its weights.

questions.question: Why might a tester distinguish "prompt injection" from ordinary "context injection" (adding retrieved text to a prompt)?

options.C: Context injection is the normal act of supplying retrieved content, while prompt injection is the malicious use of that channel to smuggle in instructions
options.A: They are two names for the exact same safe process, an idea that sounds credible in isolation but does not match the documented behaviour of these systems
options.B: Context injection is always malicious and prompt injection is always safe, a reasonable-sounding guess that does not survive scrutiny in practice
options.D: Neither term is relevant to testing, a claim that seems intuitive at first glance but does not hold up once the actual system behaviour is examined closely

questions.explanation: This reflects the underlying mechanism: context injection is the normal act of supplying retrieved content, while prompt injection is the malicious use of that channel to smuggle in instructions.

questions.question: What does "robustness" mean for a GenAI system?

options.B: The system keeps producing acceptably correct and safe output despite small or unexpected changes to the input
options.A: The system always gives the shortest possible answer, which conflates the symptom with the underlying cause of the problem
options.C: The system never needs to be retrained, which confuses two separate concepts
options.D: The system runs on any hardware, a reasonable-sounding guess that does not survive scrutiny in practice

questions.explanation: This is the defining characteristic being assessed: the system keeps producing acceptably correct and safe output despite small or unexpected changes to the input.

questions.question: What is "instruction-following" as a quality attribute?

options.D: How well the output complies with the explicit constraints given in the prompt, such as format, length, or tone
options.A: How quickly the model responds to instructions, a belief that does not match how these systems actually behave in production
options.B: Whether the model can be given more than one instruction, which confuses two separate concepts
options.C: Whether the system prompt is hidden from users, which is a frequent misreading

questions.explanation: This is the defining characteristic being assessed: how well the output complies with the explicit constraints given in the prompt, such as format, length, or tone.

questions.question: What is "helpfulness" measuring in an evaluation?

options.D: Whether the response actually assists the user in achieving their underlying goal
options.A: Whether the response is polite, which confuses two separate concepts
options.B: Whether the response uses simple vocabulary, which does not hold here
options.C: Whether the response was generated quickly, though it misses the actual cause

questions.explanation: This is the defining characteristic being assessed: whether the response actually assists the user in achieving their underlying goal, not just whether it is fluent.

questions.question: "Output diversity" as a quality attribute is most relevant when:

options.C: The task benefits from varied, non-repetitive responses, such as brainstorming or creative writing
options.A: The task requires an identical answer every time, such as arithmetic, as some teams mistakenly believe
options.B: The model is being used for factual lookup only, which confuses two separate concepts
options.D: Diversity is never a valid quality goal, which overlooks the actual mechanism driving the behaviour being tested

questions.explanation: This is the defining characteristic being assessed: the task benefits from varied, non-repetitive responses, such as brainstorming or creative writing.

questions.question: What distinguishes "safety" testing from "toxicity" testing, even though they overlap?

options.C: Safety covers a broader set of harms, such as dangerous instructions or illegal activity, while toxicity focuses specifically on hateful or abusive language
options.A: They are unrelated and never tested together, a claim that seems intuitive at first glance but does not hold up once the actual system behaviour is examined closely
options.B: Toxicity is a subset of latency testing, which might seem reasonable on the surface but is contradicted by how these systems are actually built and tested
options.D: Safety only applies to image models, which is the sort of surface-level guess that does not withstand a careful technical review of the case

questions.explanation: This is the defining characteristic being assessed: safety covers a broader set of harms, such as dangerous instructions or illegal activity, while toxicity focuses specifically on hateful or abusive language.

questions.question: What is "calibration" of a model's confidence, in simple terms?

options.A: How well the model's stated or implied confidence matches its actual likelihood of being correct
options.B: How fast the model responds under load, a reasonable-sounding guess that does not survive scrutiny in practice
options.C: How many parameters the model has, which confuses two separate concepts
options.D: How the model's temperature is set, which conflates the symptom with the underlying cause of the problem

questions.explanation: This is the defining characteristic being assessed: how well the model's stated or implied confidence matches its actual likelihood of being correct.

questions.question: Why is a low "hallucination rate" alone not sufficient evidence of good quality?

options.B: A system can have few hallucinations yet still be unhelpful, incomplete, or unsafe
options.A: Hallucination rate is not a measurable quantity, which confuses two separate concepts
options.C: A low rate proves the system is complete and safe, which does not hold here
options.D: Hallucination rate only matters for chatbots, though it misses the actual cause

questions.explanation: This is the defining characteristic being assessed: a system can have few hallucinations yet still be unhelpful, incomplete, or unsafe, so other attributes must also be measured.

questions.question: What does "fairness" testing check that a general bias check might miss?

options.B: Whether outcomes or quality of service differ systematically across specific protected or demographic groups
options.A: Whether the interface uses accessible colours, which overlooks the actual mechanism driving the behaviour being tested
options.C: Whether the model responds in under one second, which conflates the symptom with the underlying cause of the problem
options.D: Whether the model supports multiple currencies, based on a common misconception

questions.explanation: This is the defining characteristic being assessed: whether outcomes or quality of service differ systematically across specific protected or demographic groups.

questions.question: Why is "verbosity" tracked as a quality attribute for a GenAI assistant?

options.D: Overly long or overly short answers relative to what was asked can reduce usability even if the content is correct
options.A: Verbosity always indicates a factual error, which conflates the symptom with the underlying cause of the problem
options.B: Verbose answers are never a valid concern, which sounds plausible but is not supported by how the underlying mechanism works
options.C: Verbosity only matters for code generation, which overlooks the actual mechanism driving the behaviour being tested

questions.explanation: This is the defining characteristic being assessed: overly long or overly short answers relative to what was asked can reduce usability even if the content is correct.

questions.question: What is "cultural appropriateness" checking in a GenAI evaluation?

options.D: Whether responses are suitable and non-offensive across the cultural contexts the product will be used in
options.A: Whether the model supports every world language equally, a reasonable-sounding guess that does not survive scrutiny in practice
options.B: Whether the model was trained outside its home country, though it misses the actual cause
options.C: Whether the output uses formal grammar, which conflates the symptom with the underlying cause of the problem

questions.explanation: This is the defining characteristic being assessed: whether responses are suitable and non-offensive across the cultural contexts the product will be used in.

questions.question: What is a basic definition of "explainability" for a GenAI system?

options.B: The degree to which a person can understand why the system produced a particular output
options.A: The degree to which the source code is open source, based on a common misconception
options.C: The speed at which the system can be explained to a new user, though it misses the actual cause
options.D: The number of features in the user interface, though this is not accurate

questions.explanation: This is the defining characteristic being assessed: the degree to which a person can understand why the system produced a particular output.

questions.question: Why is "exploratory testing" valuable for a GenAI feature, in addition to scripted tests?

options.D: It lets testers use domain knowledge and creativity to probe unanticipated behaviours that a fixed script would not think to check
options.A: It replaces the need for any automated tests, which conflates the symptom with the underlying cause of the problem
options.B: It only works on non-AI systems, a plausible-sounding shortcut that skips over the deeper technical reason the situation actually occurred
options.C: It guarantees full coverage of all possible prompts, which overlooks the actual mechanism driving the behaviour being tested

questions.explanation: This is the sound test-design choice: it lets testers use domain knowledge and creativity to probe unanticipated behaviours that a fixed script would not think to check.

questions.question: What is a "negative test" for a GenAI assistant?

options.D: A test that supplies an invalid, out-of-scope, or disallowed input and checks the system responds appropriately, such as declining
options.A: A test that always expects the system to fail, which sounds plausible but is not supported by how the underlying mechanism works
options.B: A test written using negative numbers only, which is the sort of surface-level guess that does not withstand a careful technical review of the case
options.C: A test that disables the guardrails, a belief that does not match how these systems actually behave in production

questions.explanation: This is the sound test-design choice: a test that supplies an invalid, out-of-scope, or disallowed input and checks the system responds appropriately, such as declining.

questions.question: Why test a GenAI feature with unusually long inputs, near the context limit?

options.B: To check the system degrades safely, for example by truncating or warning
options.A: Because long inputs are the most common case in production, which does not hold here
options.C: Because long inputs always improve output quality, which testers often assume
options.D: Because the context limit does not affect quality, though this is not accurate

questions.explanation: This is the sound test-design choice: to check the system degrades safely, for example by truncating or warning, rather than failing silently or losing critical information.

questions.question: What is "combinatorial prompt testing"?

options.B: Systematically varying multiple prompt factors, such as tone, length, and language, together to cover realistic combinations efficiently
options.A: Testing only one prompt variant per release, which overlooks the actual mechanism driving the behaviour being tested
options.C: Combining several unrelated GenAI products in one test, a belief that does not match how these systems actually behave in production
options.D: Testing prompts in alphabetical order, which is the kind of assumption that leads teams astray until a proper investigation reveals the real explanation

questions.explanation: This is the sound test-design choice: systematically varying multiple prompt factors, such as tone, length, and language, together to cover realistic combinations efficiently.

questions.question: Why might a tester deliberately submit a prompt with typos or unusual spacing?

options.A: To check the system remains robust to minor, realistic input noise that real users will produce
options.B: To intentionally crash the model, which overlooks the actual mechanism driving the behaviour being tested
options.C: Because typos always improve model accuracy, which confuses two separate concepts
options.D: Because spacing has no effect on tokenization, though it misses the actual cause

questions.explanation: This is the sound test-design choice: to check the system remains robust to minor, realistic input noise that real users will produce.

questions.question: What is the "oracle problem" in GenAI testing, in simple terms?

options.B: The difficulty of deciding what counts as a correct or acceptable output when there is no single fixed expected answer
options.A: A bug in the model's training pipeline, which several teams have learned the hard way does not hold up during an actual review
options.C: A hardware limitation of GPUs, which conflates the symptom with the underlying cause of the problem
options.D: A rule that forbids automated testing, a belief that does not match how these systems actually behave in production

questions.explanation: This is the sound test-design choice: the difficulty of deciding what counts as a correct or acceptable output when there is no single fixed expected answer.

questions.question: Why should a tester check a chatbot's behaviour across a multi-turn conversation, not just single turns?

options.A: Because errors like forgetting earlier constraints or losing context often only appear after several exchanges
options.B: Because multi-turn conversations are always shorter to test, which conflates the symptom with the underlying cause of the problem
options.C: Because single-turn testing is not possible for chatbots, which confuses two separate concepts
options.D: Because multi-turn testing removes the need for any other tests, which is a frequent misreading

questions.explanation: This is the sound test-design choice: because errors like forgetting earlier constraints or losing context often only appear after several exchanges.

questions.question: What is an appropriate acceptance criterion for a task where the model must always refuse a certain request type?

options.D: The refusal rate on that request type must meet a very high threshold, measured across many repeated attempts
options.A: A single passing attempt is sufficient evidence, which conflates the symptom with the underlying cause of the problem
options.B: The refusal only needs to happen at temperature 0, which overlooks the actual mechanism driving the behaviour being tested
options.C: Refusal testing is unnecessary if the system prompt forbids it, though this is not accurate

questions.explanation: This is the sound test-design choice: the refusal rate on that request type must meet a very high threshold, measured across many repeated attempts, not just pass once.

questions.question: What is a "boundary case" for a GenAI input field with a stated maximum length?

options.A: An input right at, just under, and just over the stated maximum, to check the system handles the limit correctly
options.B: An input written in a foreign language, which conflates the symptom with the underlying cause of the problem
options.C: An input containing only punctuation, a reasonable-sounding guess that does not survive scrutiny in practice
options.D: An input that repeats the word "test", which sounds plausible but is not supported by how the underlying mechanism works

questions.explanation: This is the sound test-design choice: an input right at, just under, and just over the stated maximum, to check the system handles the limit correctly.

questions.question: Why is testing with an empty or blank prompt useful?

options.B: It reveals how the system handles missing input, such as returning a helpful message instead of an error or nonsense output
options.A: Empty prompts are not possible in real systems, which several teams have learned the hard way does not hold up during an actual review
options.C: Empty prompts always crash the model, which conflates the symptom with the underlying cause of the problem
options.D: Empty prompts are only relevant for image generation, a reasonable-sounding guess that does not survive scrutiny in practice

questions.explanation: This is the sound test-design choice: it reveals how the system handles missing input, such as returning a helpful message instead of an error or nonsense output.

questions.question: What is meant by "test design for non-determinism" in the context of this syllabus?

options.A: Designing tests and oracles that remain valid and informative even though the same input can produce different outputs
options.B: Designing tests that force the model to be fully deterministic at all times, though it misses the actual cause
options.C: Avoiding automated testing altogether, which conflates the symptom with the underlying cause of the problem
options.D: Testing only once per release, which sounds plausible but is not supported by how the underlying mechanism works

questions.explanation: This is the sound test-design choice: designing tests and oracles that remain valid and informative even though the same input can produce different outputs.

questions.question: Why might a tester compare outputs generated at different temperature settings for the same prompt?

options.C: To understand how much the sampling setting affects output variability and where instability might cause problems
options.A: Because temperature never affects test outcomes, a belief that does not match how these systems actually behave in production
options.B: Because only one temperature setting is ever used in practice, though it misses the actual cause
options.D: Because comparing settings is unrelated to quality, which conflates the symptom with the underlying cause of the problem

questions.explanation: This is the sound test-design choice: to understand how much the sampling setting affects output variability and where instability might cause problems.

questions.question: What does "exact match" measure in a QA evaluation?

options.D: Whether the model's answer is identical, character for character after light normalisation, to the reference answer
options.A: Whether the model's answer uses the same number of words, which conflates the symptom with the underlying cause of the problem
options.B: Whether the model's answer was generated instantly, a reasonable-sounding guess that does not survive scrutiny in practice
options.C: Whether the model refused to answer, which overlooks the actual mechanism driving the behaviour being tested

questions.explanation: This is the correct evaluation approach: whether the model's answer is identical, character for character after light normalisation, to the reference answer.

questions.question: What is "F1 score" commonly used for in extractive QA evaluation?

options.B: Balancing precision and recall of the predicted answer span against the reference answer
options.A: Measuring the model's file size, which conflates the symptom with the underlying cause of the problem
options.C: Measuring how many tokens were generated, which confuses two separate concepts
options.D: Measuring the temperature setting used, as some teams mistakenly believe

questions.explanation: This is the correct evaluation approach: balancing precision and recall of the predicted answer span against the reference answer.

questions.question: What is a "reference-free" evaluation method?

options.A: A scoring approach that judges an output's quality, such as fluency or groundedness, without needing a pre-written correct answer to compare against
options.B: An evaluation that ignores the input prompt, which is the sort of surface-level guess that does not withstand a careful technical review of the case
options.C: An evaluation performed without any scoring criteria, which overlooks the actual mechanism driving the behaviour being tested
options.D: An evaluation that requires no computer at all, which is the kind of assumption that leads teams astray until a proper investigation reveals the real explanation

questions.explanation: This is the correct evaluation approach: a scoring approach that judges an output's quality, such as fluency or groundedness, without needing a pre-written correct answer to compare against.

questions.question: What is a "benchmark suite" in GenAI evaluation?

options.A: A standard, structured collection of tasks and datasets used to measure and compare model or system performance
options.B: A single manually reviewed example, which conflates the symptom with the underlying cause of the problem
options.C: A list of hardware specifications, a belief that does not match how these systems actually behave in production
options.D: A tool for compressing model weights, which several teams have learned the hard way does not hold up during an actual review

questions.explanation: This is the correct evaluation approach: a standard, structured collection of tasks and datasets used to measure and compare model or system performance.

questions.question: What does "win-rate" measure in a pairwise evaluation?

options.D: The proportion of comparisons in which one system's output is judged better than the other's
options.A: The percentage of requests that succeed without errors, as some teams mistakenly believe
options.B: The number of tokens generated per second, though it misses the actual cause
options.C: The proportion of outputs that are exactly correct, which confuses two separate concepts

questions.explanation: This is the correct evaluation approach: the proportion of comparisons in which one system's output is judged better than the other's.

questions.question: Why might a team plot quality against cost when comparing model options?

options.D: To see the trade-off between response quality and the token or compute cost of achieving it, to choose an appropriate operating point
options.A: Because cost and quality are always identical, which several teams have learned the hard way does not hold up during an actual review
options.B: Because plotting is required by the exam syllabus only, an assumption that quickly breaks down once the system is tested under real conditions
options.C: Because cost has no relationship to model choice, which overlooks the actual mechanism driving the behaviour being tested

questions.explanation: This is the correct evaluation approach: to see the trade-off between response quality and the token or compute cost of achieving it, to choose an appropriate operating point.

questions.question: What is a "checklist-based" evaluation approach?

options.A: Scoring an output against a list of specific required elements or criteria, marking each as present or absent
options.B: Scoring based only on how fast the checklist was completed, though it misses the actual cause
options.C: A method that removes the need for any human review, which conflates the symptom with the underlying cause of the problem
options.D: A method usable only for code generation, though closer inspection of the system's behaviour shows this is not the case

questions.explanation: This is the correct evaluation approach: scoring an output against a list of specific required elements or criteria, marking each as present or absent.

questions.question: Why is it risky to let a model evaluate its own output without any independent check?

options.C: The model may share the same blind spots or errors as when it generated the output
options.A: Self-evaluation is always more accurate than any other method, which does not hold here
options.B: Models are legally prohibited from evaluating outputs, though this is not accurate
options.D: Self-evaluation removes the need for a rubric entirely, based on a common misconception

questions.explanation: This is the correct evaluation approach: the model may share the same blind spots or errors as when it generated the output, so self-evaluation alone can miss real defects.

questions.question: What is a reasonable evaluation cadence for a GenAI feature already in production?

options.C: A mix of continuous lightweight monitoring plus periodic deeper evaluation
options.A: Evaluation is only needed once, before the first release, which does not hold here
options.B: Evaluation should happen only when a user complains, which testers often assume
options.D: Daily full human evaluation of every request, though this is not accurate

questions.explanation: This is the correct evaluation approach: a mix of continuous lightweight monitoring plus periodic deeper evaluation, rather than testing only once before the original launch.

questions.question: What does a "scoring rubric level", for example 1 to 5, typically describe?

options.D: A defined quality band with criteria that distinguishes it from adjacent levels
options.A: The number of retries allowed for a request, though this is not accurate
options.B: The number of tokens in the response, as some teams mistakenly believe
options.C: The temperature setting used for grading, which confuses two separate concepts

questions.explanation: This is the correct evaluation approach: a defined quality band with criteria that distinguishes it from adjacent levels, so different reviewers can score consistently.

questions.question: What is "semantic similarity" scoring intended to capture that exact string matching cannot?

options.A: Whether two texts convey the same meaning, even when the wording differs
options.B: Whether two texts are stored in the same file format, though this is not accurate
options.C: Whether two texts were generated at the same temperature, which does not hold here
options.D: Whether two texts have identical length, which testers often assume

questions.explanation: This is the correct evaluation approach: whether two texts convey the same meaning, even when the wording differs.

questions.question: Why should a GenAI test dataset aim for balanced coverage across topics or domains rather than being skewed to one area?

options.C: Skewed coverage can hide weaknesses in under-represented topics and give a falsely high overall score
options.A: Balance is only a cosmetic concern with no effect on scores, which confuses two separate concepts
options.B: Skewed datasets always produce lower scores, which conflates the symptom with the underlying cause of the problem

questions.question: What is "data augmentation" in the context of building GenAI test data?

options.D: Systematically creating additional variants of existing test cases, such as paraphrases or noise, to expand coverage
options.A: Increasing the size of the production database, which sounds plausible but is not supported by how the underlying mechanism works
options.B: Adding more GPUs to the training cluster, which conflates the symptom with the underlying cause of the problem
options.C: Compressing the test dataset to save space, a reasonable-sounding guess that does not survive scrutiny in practice

questions.explanation: This is the appropriate data or environment practice: systematically creating additional variants of existing test cases, such as paraphrases or noise, to expand coverage.

questions.question: Why does "environment parity" between staging and production matter for GenAI testing?

options.C: Differences in model version, configuration, or data between environments can make staging results misleading about production behaviour
options.A: Environments are always identical by default, which overlooks the actual mechanism driving the behaviour being tested
options.B: Parity only affects UI styling, a claim that seems intuitive at first glance but does not hold up once the actual system behaviour is examined closely
options.D: Parity is unrelated to model behaviour, an assumption that quickly breaks down once the system is tested under real conditions

questions.explanation: This is the appropriate data or environment practice: differences in model version, configuration, or data between environments can make staging results misleading about production behaviour.

questions.question: What risk does "configuration drift" pose to a GenAI test environment?

options.D: Untracked changes to settings such as model version, guardrail rules, or prompt templates can make results inconsistent or non-reproducible over time
options.A: Configuration drift always improves system performance, which reflects a common but mistaken shortcut rather than the specific mechanism actually responsible here
options.B: Drift only affects network latency, which is the kind of assumption that leads teams astray until a proper investigation reveals the real explanation
options.C: Drift cannot occur once a system is deployed, a belief that does not match how these systems actually behave in production

questions.explanation: This is the appropriate data or environment practice: untracked changes to settings such as model version, guardrail rules, or prompt templates can make results inconsistent or non-reproducible over time.

questions.question: Why check the licensing terms of a dataset before using it to build or evaluate a GenAI feature?

options.B: Some datasets restrict commercial use, redistribution, or derivative works, and violating those terms creates legal risk
options.A: Licensing only applies to open-source code, never data, a belief that does not match how these systems actually behave in production
options.C: All datasets are automatically free to use for any purpose, which conflates the symptom with the underlying cause of the problem
options.D: Licensing has no bearing on testing activities, a reasonable-sounding guess that does not survive scrutiny in practice

questions.explanation: This is the appropriate data or environment practice: some datasets restrict commercial use, redistribution, or derivative works, and violating those terms creates legal risk.

questions.question: What is a "sandbox environment" used for in GenAI testing?

options.B: An isolated environment where tests, including risky or adversarial ones, can run without affecting real users or production data
options.A: A children's testing programme, though closer inspection of the system's behaviour shows this is not the case
options.C: A production environment with extra monitoring only, which several teams have learned the hard way does not hold up during an actual review
options.D: A tool for formatting test reports, an assumption that quickly breaks down once the system is tested under real conditions

questions.explanation: This is the appropriate data or environment practice: an isolated environment where tests, including risky or adversarial ones, can run without affecting real users or production data.

questions.question: Why might a tester "mock" or "stub" an external tool that an agent calls, during testing?

options.A: To get predictable, controlled responses and avoid side effects, cost, or flakiness from calling the real external service every time
options.B: Because real tools cannot be called from automated tests at all, which sounds plausible but is not supported by how the underlying mechanism works
options.C: Because mocking always makes tests less reliable, though closer inspection of the system's behaviour shows this is not the case
options.D: Because external tools do not need to be tested, which conflates the symptom with the underlying cause of the problem

questions.explanation: This is the appropriate data or environment practice: to get predictable, controlled responses and avoid side effects, cost, or flakiness from calling the real external service every time.

questions.question: What should test data curation guidelines specify for human labellers building a GenAI golden set?

options.C: Clear definitions of correctness and quality criteria, examples, and edge-case handling so labels are consistent
options.A: Only the labellers' working hours, which conflates the symptom with the underlying cause of the problem
options.B: The colour scheme of the labelling tool, which overlooks the actual mechanism driving the behaviour being tested
options.D: The number of labellers required, with no other guidance, a reasonable-sounding guess that does not survive scrutiny in practice

questions.explanation: This is the appropriate data or environment practice: clear definitions of correctness and quality criteria, examples, and edge-case handling so labels are consistent.

questions.question: Why is "seed data" curation important when bootstrapping a new GenAI evaluation set?

options.C: The initial hand-picked examples anchor quality and coverage before the set is expanded
options.A: Seed data is discarded before any evaluation begins, which does not hold here
options.B: Seed data refers only to random number generator seeds, though this is not accurate
options.D: Seed data is only relevant to model training, never evaluation, as some teams mistakenly believe

questions.explanation: This is the appropriate data or environment practice: the initial hand-picked examples anchor quality and coverage before the set is expanded, so poor seeds propagate weaknesses.

questions.question: What is a reasonable data retention practice for GenAI test transcripts containing user-like content?

options.A: Define and enforce a retention period and access controls appropriate to the sensitivity of the content
options.B: Retain all transcripts indefinitely with no access control, which confuses two separate concepts
options.C: Delete all transcripts immediately after each test run regardless of need, though this is not accurate
options.D: Retention policies are not applicable to test data, which conflates the symptom with the underlying cause of the problem

questions.explanation: This is the appropriate data or environment practice: define and enforce a retention period and access controls appropriate to the sensitivity of the content.

questions.question: Why version a "prompt dataset" separately from the application code that uses it?

options.A: Prompt datasets can change on a different cadence and by different people
